title: Gmail for teachers on Mac: templates, shortcuts and parent email in your browser
metaTitle: Gmail for Teachers on Mac: Templates, Shortcuts and Lazur
description: Gmail for teachers on Mac runs in your browser. Set up templates, keyboard shortcuts and parent replies, then ask Lazur to walk you through each step.
intro: Gmail for teachers on Mac runs in your browser, and three features do most of the work: templates, keyboard shortcuts and filters. Set them up once, and the repeat email, from parent replies to permission slip reminders, takes less effort.
tldr: Gmail on a Mac runs in your browser. Open it in Safari or Chrome, then sign in with your school account.
Turn on templates in Settings > See all settings > Advanced, then save them from any draft.
Templates work only on a computer, and a deleted template cannot be recovered.
Turn on keyboard shortcuts, press ? to see the list, and use ⌘ where Windows uses Ctrl.
Lazur points at the right button, guides you one click at a time, and dictates replies when you hold fn.

blocks.text: Gmail on a Mac runs in your browser. Google's help pages describe Gmail as a web app, and this guide follows that. Open mail.google.com in Safari or Chrome, sign in with your school account, and keep the tab open while you work. Every step below happens in that tab.
What teachers send and sort in Gmail every day

Most teacher email falls into a few groups. Parents ask about grades, schedules, missing work and permission slips. Students ask about deadlines, a missed quiz or how to submit a file. Colleagues and administrators send meeting invites, forms and policy updates. Each group repeats the same sentences, which is why saved replies pay off. The hard part is rarely the writing. It is finding the one message that needs you today.
How much time email takes teachers, and what the numbers miss

Teacher workload numbers are large, but none of them isolate email. A 2022 EdWeek Research Center survey of more than 1,300 teachers found a typical teacher works about 54 hours a week. A RAND survey of K-12 public school teachers, reported by the National Education Association, puts the figure at 53 hours. These come from different surveys, so do not merge them into one number.

No study we found measures Gmail or email time for teachers. The closest figure comes from managers and professionals. A 2022 study in the Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication found they spent 11.6 hours a week on work email during work hours. That is not a teacher number, so treat it as context, not a benchmark.

The most recent number that touches teachers and time comes from a June 2025 release by the Walton Family Foundation and Gallup. Teachers who use AI at least weekly save an average of 5.9 hours a week. The release does not name email as one of those tasks. Read it as a reason to test a tool on your own inbox, not as a promise about it.

blocks.title: Measure your own week
blocks.text: Workload surveys measure whole weeks. They do not measure how long one parent reply takes. Your own week is the best test. Track email for one ordinary week, then track it again after you turn on templates.
Turn on templates for the messages you send every week

Templates are saved messages you can drop into any compose window. Google's help page calls the feature Templates. Older guides call it canned responses. Some third-party guides describe an older menu layout. The steps below use Google's current wording, which matches the Settings menu you will see.

Start with the messages you write most often. A missing work reminder, a field trip permission slip and a conference request are good first choices. Those messages are long enough to save time and similar enough to reuse.
Step by step: turn Templates on

items: Click the gear icon at the top right of Gmail, then choose See all settings.
Open the Advanced tab on the settings page.
Find Templates and turn it on.
Click Save Changes at the bottom of the page.
Open a new compose window and click More options at the bottom. If Templates appears in the menu, the setting worked.

blocks.title: Where you will not see it
blocks.text: Templates work only on a computer. If you check mail on your phone between classes, you can read and reply there, but you cannot insert a template. Keep your template list for your Mac.
Save a template from a draft you already wrote

Say you wrote a good reply about a missing lab report. Open a new compose window and write the message. Read it once as the parent would. Then click More options at the bottom of the window, choose Templates, and select Save draft as template. Pick Save as new template, then give it a name you will recognize later, such as Missing lab report.
Before you save a template, check the details

items: Remove the student's name and grade. A template gets reused, and a name left inside goes to the next family.
Check dates and class periods. Old dates are the easiest detail to forget in reused text.
Read it as the parent would. Ask whether a stranger would know what to do next.
Keep the greeting generic. Add the parent's name after you insert the template, not inside it.
Keep formatting simple. Heavy formatting can look odd once it lands in a new message.

blocks.text: Insert, overwrite and delete templates without losing wording

To insert a template, open a new compose window and click More options at the bottom. Choose Templates, then Insert template, and pick the one you need. The text drops into the message body. Read it again before you click Send, every time. A template can fit last week and be wrong for today.

To overwrite a template, open a draft with the new wording and choose More options > Templates > Save draft as template. Under Overwrite Template, pick the old one. To delete a template, use Delete template in the same menu. Google warns that a deleted template cannot be recovered, so copy the text somewhere first.

blocks.title: Deleted means gone
blocks.text: Google's help page says a deleted template cannot be recovered. Copy the wording into a note first, then delete the template. Keep one note with your saved wording, so you can rebuild any template quickly.
Turn on Gmail keyboard shortcuts on a Mac

Gmail keyboard shortcuts are off until you turn them on. Click the gear icon, choose See all settings, and find the Keyboard shortcuts section. Select the option that turns shortcuts on, then click Save Changes. Press ? (Shift + /) at any time to open the shortcut help. Trust that list over an old blog post.
Mac keys differ from Windows keys

Google's shortcut page says shortcuts work differently on PC and Mac. Where a Windows guide says Ctrl, press ⌘ on your Mac. Some shortcuts exist only on Mac. For example, ⌘ + ; jumps to the next misspelled word. If a shortcut does nothing, check that you pressed ⌘ and not Ctrl, and that shortcuts are switched on.

items: Learn a single shortcut first. Trying everything at once is the usual reason people give up.
Keep the ? list handy for the first few days of using shortcuts.
Use shortcuts for sorting mail, not for writing. Speed matters most when you triage.
Write the shortcuts you use most on a sticky note near your keyboard.

blocks.text: Dictate parent replies instead of typing them

Hold fn to dictate. Lazur turns your speech into clean, formatted text at the cursor, in any app. Put the cursor in the Gmail body, hold fn, and talk the reply the way you would say it at the front desk. Release fn, read it back, then send. Dictation is unlimited on both Pro and Power.

Dictation can miss proper names. A parent's last name, a student's nickname or a colleague's first name can come out wrong. Use the personal dictionary for words you use often, such as a school name or a course code. Keep student records out of it.
Snippets and clipboard slots for text you reuse

Snippets and clipboard slots cover text that templates do not handle well. A template lives inside Gmail. A snippet can help with text you use outside Gmail too, such as a room number or a course code. Keep long policy text in Gmail templates, where it stays with the emails that use it.
What Lazur does in Gmail, and what it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant that lives in the notch of your Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a button is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. You press Send. Lazur also handles everyday jobs by voice, including timers, Apple Reminders, Calendar events, notes, music and volume, opening apps and links, web search and Shortcuts.
Privacy rules for teachers using AI on screen

Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those are the product's stated rules. Your school's data policy still decides what you may share, so check it before you put student names or records on screen.

A practical rule helps here. If you would not read the screen aloud in a staff room, do not ask Lazur about it. Hold the shortcut only when you need help with that screen, and close any record you no longer need.

blocks.text: Sort class and school mail with filters and labels

A filter sorts mail before you see it. Filters work well for a school newsletter, a department list or a district form. Pick one sender or one phrase, decide where the mail goes, then test the filter on a real message. Labels give you a place to keep what matters, such as a folder for one unit.

Start with the [filter guide](/how-to/create-a-filter-in-gmail) and the [label guide](/how-to/create-a-label-in-gmail). Add one filter at a time. A filter that is too broad can hide a parent email you need today.
A worked example: one Friday inbox

Take a Friday after school as an example. Open Gmail and start with parent mail. Read each message, reply with a template where one fits, and dictate anything that needs a personal touch. Archive the messages you finish, using the [archive guide](/how-to/archive-emails-in-gmail) if you are new to it.

Move to student mail next. Those messages usually need a short answer about a deadline or a file. Colleagues come last, because most of their messages can wait until Monday. Snooze anything that needs a decision after the weekend, using the [snooze guide](/how-to/snooze-an-email-in-gmail).
Ask Lazur at each step if you forget a shortcut. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask, and Lazur answers out loud or points at the button. Keep the thread on screen, so Lazur can see what you mean.
Edge cases: shared Macs and school accounts

Templates belong to the Google account you sign in with. If you share a Mac, sign out of Gmail when you finish, so the next person does not see your school mail. If your school account does not show the Advanced tab, ask the person who runs your school's Google accounts. That is faster than guessing.

Phone and Mac work differently here. You can read mail on a phone and reply there, but your Mac templates do not show up on the phone. Plan your reusable replies at your Mac, then use the phone for quick reading.
Common mistakes teachers make in Gmail

items: Expecting templates on a phone. Google says they work only on a computer.
Deleting a template without copying it first. Deleted templates cannot be recovered.
Pressing Ctrl on a Mac. Shortcuts use ⌘ where Windows uses Ctrl.
Sending a saved reply with the last family's name still in it.
Turning on shortcuts, then forgetting the ? list exists.
Expecting Lazur to do the clicking. Lazur points and guides, and you press each button.

blocks.text: If a message went to the wrong person, act quickly. The [recall guide](/how-to/recall-a-sent-email-in-gmail) explains what works and what does not, so read it before you try anything.
A first week with Gmail on your Mac

items: Turn on templates from Settings > See all settings > Advanced, then save.
Save the messages you send most often as templates.
Turn on keyboard shortcuts, then press ? once to see the list.
Set one filter for the sender whose mail you open first.
Ask Lazur to walk you through any step that stalls.

faq.question: Is there an official Gmail app for Mac?
faq.answer: Google's help pages describe Gmail in a browser, and this guide uses Safari or Chrome. Open mail.google.com and sign in. If Google releases a Mac app later, the menu names here may change, so check Google's help pages for current steps.

faq.question: Do templates work on my iPhone?
faq.answer: Not according to Google's help page. You can only turn on and use templates from Gmail on a computer, not the mobile apps. Plan your reusable replies at your Mac, then read mail on the phone if you need to.

faq.question: Can I get a deleted template back?
faq.answer: No. Google warns that deleted templates cannot be recovered. Copy the wording into a note before you delete anything.

faq.question: How many templates can I save?
faq.answer: Google's template page does not state a maximum number. Start with the messages you send most. Add more only when you catch yourself retyping the same text.

faq.question: Why are my keyboard shortcuts not working?
faq.answer: Shortcuts must be turned on in Settings. Open Settings > See all settings, select the shortcuts option under Keyboard shortcuts, and click Save Changes. Then use ⌘ where Windows uses Ctrl.

faq.question: Can Lazur send my email for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur guides, points, explains, answers out loud, drafts and types text. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. You read the message and press Send.

faq.question: Is it safe to use Lazur with student information?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you and are not stored. Check your school's data policy before you share student records.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.
